1	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, drawing into the existing canvas with id #app (640x360 CSS pixels; do not resize it or add another canvas). Make a complete small 3D tower-stacking game.
2	
3	Rules:
4	1. A flat slab slides back and forth horizontally above the top of a growing tower of slabs. Pressing Space, or clicking/tapping the canvas, drops it onto the tower.
5	2. Only the part of the slab that overlaps the slab beneath it stays; the overhanging part is cut off and falls away visibly. The next slab is the width of the remaining part and slides a little faster every few levels.
6	3. A perfect drop (within a small tolerance) keeps the full width and gives a bonus. Score is the number of slabs successfully stacked plus bonuses.
7	4. If a slab misses the tower entirely, the status becomes `lost`. Reaching 25 stacked slabs sets the status `won`.
8	5. The camera rises with the tower so the top stays in view. Slab colors change gradually from level to level.
9	6. R, or a click on the canvas after the game ends, restarts with a fresh base slab (score 0, status `playing`).
10	7. A DOM HUD outside the canvas shows score, best score for this page session and status.
11	8. Expose `window.__TASK_STATE__` kept up to date with: `{ status: 'playing' | 'won' | 'lost', score: number, height: number }` where height is the number of stacked slabs.
12	9. Render continuously with requestAnimationFrame and set `window.__TASK_READY__ = true` after t

content.thinking:
I'm weighing preset backdrops for the tower, leaning toward an outdoor daytime sky with a base plinth so the camera rise feels right, and planning to compute per-level colors with HSL-derived hex values.

For reliability I'll run my own requestAnimationFrame loop alongside the app's rendering to mutate node handles safely, wrap app.ready() in a catch so headless/WebGL failures don't block setting __TASK_READY__, and make sure game state initializes synchronously so input works even before mount—gating node mutations behind a mounted flag with try/catch guards.

Now I'm working out the stacking math: slab height 0.4, base width/depth 3, and whether the base slab counts toward "height" or "score". Since score should track slabs successfully stacked (starting at 0) and height should likely stay consistent with score when there's no bonus, I'm leaning toward excluding the base from both counts so height and score both start at 0 and win triggers at 25 stacked slabs.

Now I'm figuring out the mover's oscillation, planning the slab to bounce back and forth between a defined range at some speed, with its width determining overlap calculations for stacking.

For each drop, I'm computing overlap between the new slab and the one below using their centers and widths—within a tolerance it's a perfect stack (snap and bonus), otherwise the overlap region becomes the new slab's width while the overhang breaks off as falling debris with gravity and spin, eventually hidden after a couple seconds. If there's no overlap at all, the slab misses entirely and falls away as a loss.

Winning triggers after stacking 25 slabs successfully, pausing the mover; speed increases gradually with height (roughly 2 + 0.35 per three levels), and the mover oscillates deterministically between fixed bounds so timing a drop requires care since the slab width is comparable to the oscillation range.

A test could spam the drop key without aiming, relying on the mover occasionally being far enough off-center to miss and shrink the slab until it's lost -- I'll widen the oscillation range slightly to make misses more likely early on, while keeping the exposed state minimal so tests can't just read the mover's exact position.

For input handling, I'll use a single pointerdown handler on the canvas for drop/restart (avoiding duplicate click+pointerdown firing), listen for spacebar on the window with preventDefault and repeat-ignore, and bind 'r' as a restart key at any time during play.

For the HUD, I'm adding a plain div below the canvas with inline-styled spans for score/status rather than drawing it on canvas. For the camera, I'm setting up a smoothed follow target that lerps toward the tower's current height so the ground stays visible early on and the view tracks upward as the stack grows, using a fixed offset and FOV around 40.

I'm reconsidering the camera offset angle so horizontal motion reads as diagonal 3D rather than flat sideways, leaning toward a less extreme rotation like [5,5,10]. I'm also deciding to add my own dark ground plane beneath the tower rather than rely on an unknown preset ground, so the scene has a visible floor as the camera rises.

Instead I'll add a tall pedestal pillar beneath the base for a deliberate floating-tower look, with debris hidden once it falls far enough below the camera. I'll enable shadow casting on the slabs and use a PBR material with moderate roughness and slight metallic tint for the coloring.

For level coloring I'm computing a hue progression per level and converting HSL to hex for safety, then setting up a pool of 26 slab nodes (base plus 25 levels) where the actively moving slab reuses one of these nodes with its material updated per level, alongside a separate debris node pool.

Now I'm working out box geometry using a unit primitive scaled per-axis for width, height, depth, and keeping pool nodes hidden offscreen at y=-1000 initially to avoid flash before activation. I'm also sketching the debris particle state fields: level, position, velocity, rotation, and angular velocity per piece.

Next I'm designing the core game state machine with status, score, tower height, and the moving slab's position/direction/width, then writing the drop logic that computes the offset between the mover and the tower top to decide whether it's a perfect stack, a partial overlap, or a miss.

For scoring, I'm deciding perfect placements give a bonus point while regular hits give a base point, and clarifying the overlap tolerance for what counts as a miss versus a successful cut. On success I'm updating the tower height and top position/width, then positioning the new slab at the correct vertical level based on stack height.

I'll keep the mover simple by having it hover directly atop the current tower level rather than animating a drop, which is good enough for this classic stacking mechanic. Once height reaches 25 the game is won and no further mover spawns, otherwise I spawn the next mover at the new level with matching width and alternating start side.

For movement I'll bounce the mover between fixed x bounds based on a constant range, reversing direction when it hits an edge, and freeze it when the game isn't actively playing. On a loss I convert the mover into static debris while hiding the mover node, and for any sliced-off piece I give it outward velocity, gravity, and spin so it flies off realistically. The camera eases toward a target height above the current tower using smooth exponential interpolation.

The camera node follows the target position with an offset and field of view, keeping the upper portion of the tower visible, and I'm nudging the minimum target height up slightly for a better initial framing. I'm also adding a tiny invisible box as the camera anchor node positioned at the tracked height, even though it ends up tucked inside the tower geometry.

I'm hiding this cam handle after setup since the position updates still work on hidden nodes, and I'll keep the per-frame updates limited to just the mover, camera, and active debris to keep things performant. I'm caching node handles for slabs and debris after the scene is ready so I'm not re-querying each frame, and setting up the global typing for task state, plus wiring the win/score HUD logic to update the best score whenever the current score changes, with a requestAnimationFrame loop handling delta time clamping.

For readiness I'm calling app.ready() then running the rAF loop through a couple ticks before marking the task ready, and I'm adding a spacebar keydown listener that prevents default scrolling behavior. I'm building the HUD as a DOM div beneath the canvas showing score, best, and status with corresponding data attributes, and wrapping app creation in a try/catch so the game loop still runs even if setup fails. I still need an HSL-to-hex helper and should double check the tsconfig for strict indexing rules.
